children: Tanya Pandey A call by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to slow the pace of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development has opened up a much wider debate over how fast the technology should advance. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, xAI chief Elon Musk, Microsoft chief Satya Nadella and even the United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk have since joined Dario to call for a pause, as concerns over AI safety meet questions around the cost of building frontier models, the loss of jobs, impact on the environment along with its use for autonomous and dangerous weapons.

But are the calls for pacing development genuinely about bringing in greater oversight or is a ploy for a cover up, Tanya Pandey explains. What are the calls for a slowdown, what do they comprise? The calls are not for stopping AI development. They are about giving safety testing and oversight more time to keep up with increasingly capable models, through independent evaluations, common safety standards, and greater coordination between companies and governments.

Why is it an issue now? AI systems are becoming more autonomous and are taking on tasks that previously required humans. They are also increasingly being used to write code and help develop other AI systems, raising concerns that capabilities could improve faster than companies can understand and control them. Former employees of some of these labs have come out in the open to express concerns and have even warned that AI could kill humans by end of this decade.

Could the slowdown also protect big AI labs? As Chinese open-weight models such as Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen and Z.ai's GLM become increasingly capable at a fraction of the cost of leading US models, tighter government controls could make it harder for smaller companies and open source developers to compete with the biggest labs.

Some critics argue this could help the leading AI companies retain their advantage. How is the market reacting to the calls? The AI boom has created a huge investment chain around chips, data centres and computing infrastructure. Investors are now assessing what a slower pace of frontier AI development could mean for that spending. SoftBank fell as much as 13.2%, while Kioxia, SK Hynix, Samsung, TSMC and Tokyo Electron also declined.

Is the AI industry also facing an economic problem? The cost of training frontier models has risen massively. Training some of the largest models now costs hundreds of millions of dollars, with future frontier training runs expected to cross $1 billion. At the same time, open source models are becoming more capable and cheaper, raising questions over whether frontier labs can keep spending at this pace.

How does the AI slowdown tie into the US-China race? The argument is that the US should maintain its lead while putting safeguards around frontier development, alongside tighter controls on advanced AI technology going to China. Beijing has rejected that approach, with its Foreign Ministry saying that "fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition" would disrupt global AI governance.

What do IPO plans tell us about AI industry's position? The slowdown debate comes as biggest AI labs face massive commercial expectations. OpenAI has pushed its IPO plans out of 2026, after reportedly eyeing a valuation of around $1 trillion. Anthropic is preparing for a potential IPO and is reportedly seeking a valuation of over $2 trillion.

title: Code of Conduct Only for Smaller Cos?
